title: Relative clauses + こと/の + とき

grammarPoints.rule: A relative clause in Japanese is just a sentence parked in front of a noun. There is no "that", no "which", no "who" — you put the whole sentence there and the noun it lands in front of is what the sentence is about. 「ほんを みる」 is a sentence; 「ほんを みる ひと」 is the person who looks at books. Nothing is added and nothing is reordered. One rule only: the verb inside the clause stays PLAIN. ます is the politeness of the whole SENTENCE, and it can only ever sit on the last verb — never inside a clause.

examples.ja: ほんを みる ひとが いる。
examples.en: There is a person who looks at books.

examples.ja: ちゃを のむ ひとは ミカだ。
examples.en: The person who drinks tea is Mika.

examples.ja: うみで およぐ ひとが すきだ。
examples.en: I like people who swim in the sea.

examples.ja: ごはんを たべる じかんが ない。
examples.en: There is no time to eat.

examples.ja: きっさてんで はたらく ひとと あそぶ。
examples.en: I hang out with the person who works at the coffee shop.

antiPattern.ja: ほんを みます ひとが いる。
antiPattern.why: the verb inside a clause stays PLAIN — ます is the politeness of the whole sentence and only ever sits on the LAST verb: ほんを みる ひとが いる。

grammarPoints.rule: Put the clause in the past and nothing else changes — the plain past sits in front of the noun exactly where the plain non-past did. 「きのう かった ほん」 = the book I bought yesterday. Who did the buying is usually left out and the rest of the sentence makes it obvious. And there is never a の between the clause and its noun: の joins two NOUNS (ミカの ほん), never a clause to the noun it describes.

examples.ja: きのう かった ほんを みた。
examples.en: I looked at the book I bought yesterday.

examples.ja: あさ のんだ ちゃは おいしい。
examples.en: The tea I drank in the morning is delicious.

examples.ja: きのう いった みせは ふるい。
examples.en: The shop I went to yesterday is old.

examples.ja: きのう きいた うたが すきだ。
examples.en: I like the song I heard yesterday.

examples.ja: きのう たべた すしは たかい。
examples.en: The sushi I ate yesterday is expensive.

antiPattern.ja: きのう かった の ほんを みた。
antiPattern.why: の joins two NOUNS — it never joins a clause to the noun it describes, so the clause sits straight in front: きのう かった ほんを みた。

grammarPoints.rule: Give the clause its own subject and that subject takes が: 「ミカが かった ほん」 = the book Mika bought. The が belongs to the clause alone and never reaches outside it. は cannot go there. は marks the topic of the WHOLE sentence and a sentence gets one topic, so a は inside a clause collides with the one outside it. Rule of thumb while you learn this: outside the clause は, inside the clause が.

examples.ja: わたしは ミカが かった ほんを みた。
examples.en: I looked at the book Mika bought.

examples.ja: ケンが きいた うたは おもしろい。
examples.en: The song Ken heard is interesting.

examples.ja: たなかが おしえる じゅぎょうは おもしろい。
examples.en: The class Tanaka teaches is interesting.

examples.ja: ミカが かった いえは しずかだ。
examples.en: The house Mika bought is quiet.

examples.ja: わたしが かった かばんは やすい。
examples.en: The bag I bought is cheap.

antiPattern.ja: わたしは ミカは かった ほんを みた。
antiPattern.why: one sentence, one は — the clause's own subject takes が instead: わたしは ミカが かった ほんを みた。

grammarPoints.rule: You already turn a verb into a thing with の — 「たべるのが すきだ」. こと does the identical job: 「たべる ことが すきだ」. And it is the same shape you have been building all module — a plain clause in front of a noun — except the noun is こと, "the act of", so the clause becomes something you can like, hate, or make the subject of a sentence. Both are right; の is the spoken half and こと the written half. こと is also an ordinary noun meaning "thing" in the abstract sense: 「わからない ことが ある」 = there is something I don't understand.

examples.ja: うみで およぐ ことが すきだ。
examples.en: I like swimming in the sea.

examples.ja: ほんを みる ことが すきだ。
examples.en: I like looking at books.

examples.ja: あさ はたらく ことは きらいだ。
examples.en: I hate working in the morning.

examples.ja: ともだちと あそぶ ことは おもしろい。
examples.en: Hanging out with friends is fun.

examples.ja: わからない ことが ある。
examples.en: There is something I don't understand.

antiPattern.ja: うみで およぐが すきだ。
antiPattern.why: a verb cannot be marked が on its own — こと (or の) turns it into a thing first: うみで およぐ ことが すきだ。

grammarPoints.rule: とき is just the noun "time", and by now you know how to describe a noun: park a clause in front of it. 「にほんに いく とき」 = the time when I go to Japan → when I go to Japan. What sits in front follows the same rules as everything else that describes a noun — a verb goes in plain, a noun takes の (がくせいの とき = when I was a student), a な-adjective takes な (げんきな とき). While you are learning it, keep the two halves in the same tense: a 〜る とき clause with a non-past sentence, a 〜た とき clause with a past one.

examples.ja: がくせいの とき じてんしゃを かった。
examples.en: When I was a student, I bought a bicycle.

examples.ja: ごはんを たべる とき みずを のむ。
examples.en: When I eat, I drink water.

examples.ja: きっさてんに いった とき ちゃを のんだ。
examples.en: When I went to the coffee shop, I drank tea.

examples.ja: うみに いく とき ぼうしを かう。
examples.en: When I go to the sea, I buy a hat.

examples.ja: げんきな とき うみで およぐ。
examples.en: When I'm well, I swim in the sea.

antiPattern.ja: がくせいだ とき じてんしゃを かった。
antiPattern.why: だ never sits in front of a noun — a noun describing another noun takes の: がくせいの とき じてんしゃを かった。

grammarPoints.rule: まえ means "before". Put a clause in front of it — the same shape as always — add に, and you have "before doing X": 「だいがくに いく まえに ごはんを たべる」 = before going to university, I eat. Here is the piece that catches everybody: the verb in front of まえに is ALWAYS the dictionary form, even when the whole thing happened yesterday. まえに only says "earlier than"; the tense is decided by the verb at the END of the sentence. 「たべた まえに」 is never Japanese. A noun takes の, as usual: 「じゅぎょうの まえに」.

examples.ja: だいがくに いく まえに ごはんを たべる。
examples.en: Before going to university, I eat.

examples.ja: ちゃを のむ まえに ほんを みた。
examples.en: Before drinking tea, I looked at a book.

examples.ja: きっさてんに いく まえに かばんを かった。
examples.en: Before going to the coffee shop, I bought a bag.

examples.ja: じゅぎょうの まえに ともだちと あそんだ。
examples.en: Before class, I hung out with a friend.

examples.ja: うみで およぐ まえに みずを のんだ。
examples.en: Before swimming in the sea, I drank water.

antiPattern.ja: だいがくに いった まえに ごはんを たべる。
antiPattern.why: まえに always takes the DICTIONARY form, whatever the tense of the sentence — the verb at the end carries the tense: だいがくに いく まえに ごはんを たべる。

grammarPoints.rule: The other half of the pair. Take the て-form you already own, hang から on it, and you have "after doing X": 「ごはんを たべてから だいがくに いく」 = after eating, I go to university. て on its own already links actions in the order they happen; てから adds that the first one is FINISHED before the second starts. The tense still lives on the last verb only — 「たべてから いった」 = after eating, I went. And the pair is complete: まえに takes the dictionary form, てから takes the て-form.

examples.ja: ごはんを たべてから だいがくに いく。
examples.en: After eating, I go to university.

examples.ja: うたを きいてから ごはんを たべた。
examples.en: After listening to a song, I ate.

examples.ja: きっさてんに いってから みせに いった。
examples.en: After going to the coffee shop, I went to the shop.

examples.ja: ちゃを のんでから しゃしんを みた。
examples.en: After drinking tea, I looked at the photo.

examples.ja: めがねを かってから えきに いった。
examples.en: After buying glasses, I went to the station.

antiPattern.ja: ごはんを たべるてから だいがくに いく。
antiPattern.why: から hangs on the て-form, not the dictionary form — たべる becomes たべて first: ごはんを たべてから だいがくに いく。
